review_text: I took this class in Spring 2021. Typically, while most people say that your 451 grade with Kruskal is the same as your 351 grade with Kruskal, I feel as though your 451 grade may be lower. If you choose to take this class with Kruskal, be sure you know what you're doing... Pros: + The ridiculously long pre lecture videos from 351 are gone. The professor actually teaches new content during lecture time, making lectures highly informative. + He repeats most NP assignments from 351, so you can reuse your work + Professor is very chill regarding deadlines. Often, he would extend a homework deadline by a few dates simply because someone asked nicely. Our midterm deadline was actually moved by 2 weeks. Cons: - The quizzes from 351 that helped gauge your progress are (mostly) gone. We had a few at the beginning of the semester but they stopped afterwards - There are no written solutions given for any homework assignment (not just NP). This is especially detrimental when exams are often based off of homework assignments. While there are review sessions that go over homework assignments, they lack the formal rigor that a written solution would have. Also, there is no guarantee that the every problem is covered in these sessions. It is especially baffling that we do not have solution keys when this was done so often back in 351. - The live lectures are often very free-flowing and not directed without the slide set. This can make it difficult to determine what to take notes on. - No review material is given for either the midterm or final. The homework assignments do not make up for this. As a result, it is very easy to lose lots of points of exam questions where you may actually understand the concepts at hand. Again, exam review material is something that was easily made for 351, so I am shocked that they couldn't apply the same processes here to make it.
evidence_snippet: exams are often based off homework assignments
label_rationale: Exams depend heavily on homework, while missing solutions and review materials create confusion.

review_text: Before I get into my review, I should note that the C+ is pretty much entirely on me. I should have taken the course more seriously, especially for the first midterm, and I got burned for not doing so. At least I passed. With that said, this class did not work for me whatsoever. It's not because the class is hard, though it absolutely is, and I'd argue it should be. I just don't think it's for the right reasons. For instance, the lecture/exam half of the course is almost entirely disjoint from the GeekOS project half of the course, and it really feels like a 5/6 credit course sometimes. Being good at the lecture content will not help you whatsoever with GeekOS, and vice versa. This seems to be a 412-wide issue. Regarding the lecture content, I don't think Pete is a very good lecturer. It's sort of what the other reviewers this semester so far have pointed out. I wouldn't quite agree with the tin can rattling mentality, but he certainly doesn't practice his presentations, and he brings absolutely no energy to the class. Another reviewer pointed out the ChatGPT image, which he said he would fix and never did, but there was another instance where he took a TRIO slide set from the internet, didn't review it at all beforehand, and tried going through it in a rather miserable showing. There's very little transformation of his slide content in his lectures, as all he does is take his laser pointer and point to things he wants to emphasize on one of the projectors in the room. The slides themselves are rather poor summaries of OSTEP, which he follows very closely. That's just lectures themselves. The assignments he gives aren't much better in my opinion. He assigns weekly Gradescope reading homeworks which are worth 1% of the grade each. I honestly almost wish he would give more traditional homeworks instead. Some of the questions are horribly ambiguous, there's no room to state any assumptions, there are some questions where it feels like even with both the slides and OSTEP you can't really answer well, they ultimately lack engagement, and they are nowhere near comprehensive enough to actually prepare for the exams imo. Regarding exams, exam 1 was insane with the short answer questions of random topics from the slides being worth so much of the grade, while exams 2 and 3, especially 3, were relatively more chill. These certainly weren't my strongsuit, as I'm horrible with memorizing topics which I haven't worked directly with in some meaningful way, and I'm rather terrible at studying. I didn't like them, but they were fine I guess. One question I would like to address is the barber shop semaphore problem in exam 2. Not only were the semantics poorly defined, as the professor admitted, but in my experience, semaphore programming isn't just something just I get right away. I haven't worked with them before, as I haven't had any need to. They really weren't gone over well in class, nor were the gradescope assignments enough to really nail it in. He didn't give any other practice problem on them besides the baboon problem from a reading homework. I realize this is just one specific example, but it's emblematic of my problem with this part of the class as a whole. I also realize this could just be me, and my review should be taken with at least a grain of salt due to my meager performance compared to the rest of the class. I didn't mention this before, but each exam was 15%, and there was no final exam. Regarding GeekOS, the TA's, especially Leo, really carried here. They were really helpful in getting some of the projects working, and I really wouldn't have passed the class without them. Though, I'd maybe argue they were a bit too necessary to get through the projects. It's very clear the project specs haven't been updated in years, and the project slides, especially for the later projects such as 4b and all of 5, don't seem at all sufficient in getting you through the projects. Of course, the projects should be challenging, but in my experience, there was a lot of frustration due to how much information the slides and specs omit. For example, in project 5, file systems, GFS3 is a completely proprietary file system, yet we're not really given a good specification of it. For example, we were only given one example GFS3 image whose structure is completely undocumented. In project 4b, demand paging (the hardest project imo, though I hated 5 more just by nature), the way in which we were basically required to do things isn't very easy to deduce from source code, and the slides honestly made it more confusing what we had to do. Don't get me wrong, these projects are pretty cool at the end of the day, and honestly it was very useful being forced to navigate and implement significant components into a Linux-like kernel. I just think the projects would be better if the provided resources were more helpful. Finally, there's grading. The class is graded on a curve. This semester, seemingly a lot of insanely smart people took the class, which seemingly skewed the grade distribution like crazy. There was a review last semester of someone getting an 88 with Dr. Agrawala and ending with an A+. I know someone who got like an 89 this semester and ended with an A-. Take that for what you will. Overall, I can't say I don't recommend taking this class at all, but I have some issues with it. Pete is teaching this class next spring, so it seems for a little bit, Dr. Agrawala and Pete are alternating teaching this class.

review_text: Dr. Yoon's delightful attitude towards student concerns was not enough to fully recommend him as a lecturer. This course is pretty dry and dull in terms of material, so I am not sure if any other teacher would've made it more interesting for me, but Dr. Yoon certainly did not. I felt so inadequately prepared for both exams, and the homeworks were tedious busy work. On top of that he assigned a coding project in C that was a simulation of the MIPS pipeline process (You learn about this during the class) and it was the second hardest project I ever took on and I felt it was just useless busy work. The midterm was incredibly long and ridiculously packed with material not many were familiar with. He even said he anticipated low exam scores because people would not finish on time. For the first exam, we originally had 85 minutes, however since there was no class after ours let out he extended it to 100 minutes because people needed more time. This was the same situation for the final exam only no time extension. I barely got time to go to all the questions and just attempt them. The one thing that makes this class with Yoon worth it, is it can be a passable class since he gives a butt load of extra credit and partial credit for just attempting questions but not necessarily answering them correctly. Because of the unreasonable amount of questions on exams, the difficulty of the project and homeworks, the average of the class was a 56%. So Yoon curved the course NICELY. I ended up with a 66% and that was good enough for a B- . I like Yoon as a person and he's very helpful in his office hours but he still isn't very clear on the material a lot of times. Since I do not know how the other teachers are for 411 I cannot suggest taking them over Yoon. If you have to take Yoon just remember these things 1) The exams are unreasonably long and nearly impossible to get an A on, but he gives a lot of partial credit for simply attempting questions. 2) The project he assigns is hard and unnecessary busy work. 3) He isn't very effective as a lecturer, and does not give enough resources and practice materials to prepare you for exams. Even homeworks are not sufficient.

review_text: As a student, I was incredibly interested in the possibility of taking an artificial intelligence course at UMD. However the biggest thing that was a let down was the way the course was instructed and the instructors themselves. Max is most definitely incredibly knowledged about the subject, and seems to have a passion for AI itself. However, the course was by far the worst organized 400 level course I have taken at UMD, and that's coming from a university with many "below average" professors in the computer science department. First and foremost, no enforcement of the material was given throughout the year. The course "material" was directly copied and ripped off from CS188, Berkeley's Intro to AI course. The slides, were directly copied as well. As a student, I found it much more effective to visit Berkeley's website and learn from their instructors instead. Signing up for this course would be a waste of your tuition when you can simply learn the material yourself using the CS188 website. Even the midterm itself was given with a low effort on the instructors part. The midterm was given online in class. Almost all students found the midterm to be impossible to complete in the given time, and this resulted in a low average for the exam. Instructors had to remove an entire section of the midterm after grading to better curve the results, which meant that students spent time on that section for no reason. There were 3 total homeworks given in the class. Homeworks 2 and 3 provided more of a learning experience and had more applicability to the course material in comparison to anything else we'd ever learned in class. Homework 3 was building an image classifier using a nueral network which ended up being the most helpful and interesting project done in the class. This project was done using PyTorch, however Max provided absolutely no guidance on how to start with PyTorch leading students to self learn the material before being able to start the homework itself. The final project was a group project, but yet again students were misinformed of the requirements. We were orginally told to complete a short report on our project, but a week before the deadline, this was changed to a 3-5 page report. Moreover, the grading procedure of the final project was not given until a week before the deadline. The lack of communication and help with both the homeworks and the final project speaks to how poorly the class was run. Overall, it seems that some individuals are not meant to teach no matter how knowledgable they are in the material, and Max is one of them.
evidence_snippet: leading students to self learn...final project...requirements changed
label_rationale: Students self-learned project tools while facing impossible exams and shifting project requirements.

Regarding the actual lectures, they are really boring, but I wouldn't expect anything else from a computer science lecture. The pace of the lecture is quite fast, and if you are not a fast writer (like me), then you are in a bit of trouble, and most of your notes will end up looking like chicken scratch. For the first month or so of class it will drag on if you take this class right after CMSC131 due to the fact that a good amount of the lectures at the beginning of the class just recap old CMSC131, but I wouldn't get too comfortable with that since it does quickly move onto new content that you will need for the exams and projects. While on the topic of the exams, they are absolutely some of the most difficult exams I've taken in college. I have plenty of gripes with his exams, the first of these is that for the multiple-choice section of the exams, he will take points off if you select the wrong answer instead of the question just not giving credit. Because of this grading policy, I've had one of his exams go from a high D (still a low grade, I know) to a high E. Along with that, the content on these exams is very difficult, from the coding questions to the multiple choice questions, after you leave the exam room, it will have you wondering if you even studied for it. Also, on some occasions, the practice exams that he gives are nothing like the actual exam, so if you use the practice exam to study and he decides to change up the format, then you are doomed. Onto some of the positives of Herman's class, he does try to break up the monotony of his class by joking around with the students and just throwing a couple of jokes here and there to break it up. Also, he uses the students sitting in the front row to use as examples for how different concepts work, which ends up being a lot more informative than him just talking and talking about it with some slides on the screen. Overall, Larry Herman is an alright instructor (if you take this class do not call him professor) with some odd policies that make sense when yuo really think about them, but he also has a fair share of negatives to consider before registering for his class. review_text: Now, Neil is a great guy and a somewhat competent teacher. His teaching style takes getting used to; he basically walks into class everyday, opens up VI and just types notes, which you are expected to copy down and know. If you take notes on paper, learn to do it by computer, or you will get crazy pissed when he hops all over the place modifying what he wrote. My personal suggestion is Microsoft OneNote. Of course, he posts the notes file online, so you don't really need to take notes, but I would advise you do so, particularly if you're not that familiar with the subject. He involves the class by basically asking us questions and writing the answers in his VI file. He writes it very colloquially which is nice, but sometimes he uses really obnoxiously large, outmoded words (draconian, pathological etc.). The way the lectures go will be entirely up to you and your classmates. In my case, my classmates were total geniuses. We have 1 guy who got a diploma from MIT, half the robotics team, and a bunch of other people who basically know everything there is to know about linux. These people will be the bane of your existence if you are not one of them. They will side track the class, ask really convoluted and (in my opinion) irrelevant questions, and basically confuse the HELL out of you. It is basically your job to slow these people down and make sure they don't get too many opportunities to derail the class. Neil also gives quizzes if someone's cell phone goes off in the class. So, study your notes every night basically. He also has a huge vocab sheet he posts at the beginning of the semester, with words that will be covered on his multiple choice exams. Now some of you may have seen me say multiple choice, and grinned happily; set aside that notion, Neil's exams are pretty damn bad. His questions are more tricks than tests of knowledge, there are several that can be interpreted to mean different things, and it's really anyone's guess as to what they truly ask. Other questions can sometimes reword the answers in such a way that even if you know what the answer is, finding them among the choices is tricky. The projects in this course are pure hell for the most part with 1 or 2 exceptions. This isn't really Neil's fault, he delegated it all to his TA, who mismanaged time a fair amount (routinely showed lecture slides for projects 3 weeks before they were ASSIGNED). Overall, it's not easy to review this course, as I don't know if it's me, the TA, the professor, or the course itself that's the problem, but I do put in 40 ish hours a week for out of class work, and I have a C-. Neil is a fair guy though, so I am not too worried about failing/passing. If you want an A in this class, and haven't been weaned on linux, then you will need to start reading the book weeks before the semester begins. Make sure you have flashcards ready from a previous semester on DAY ONE of the class. Look over previous semester's projects. This class is more demanding than any other I have ever taken, and it's in no small part because of the disparity in intelligence of the individuals who take it. It's going to be a tough, long, hard semester, but keep your head up, and prepare well, and you will get the grade you earn. If your time management sucks, however, prepare for a real shock to the system; this is one of the hardest courses offered at UMD, and you will find out why.

This professor does not teach, and it feels like he does not care about this class at all. He was not present at the midterm to answer questions, and when we asked the TA's questions at the midterm, they said "Let me ask the Professor" and then the professor would not respond, so the TA's did their best in answering our questions for the midterm. Every homework assignment released with bugs, meaning if you wanted to start the homework early, you'd have to post on piazza about the bug, wait for the TA's to fix it, and then start again. Every homework assignment had extremally vague instructions and grading criteria spawning many questions on the piazza. These questions were often answered by complete non answers, or "you should know this". Might I add that the in person question sessions were not recorded, so if you could not remember what a TA/Professor said during class, there was no way to get that answer. So, if they answered a piazza question in class, you're just left hoping another student will answer it for you. In completing the homeworks, many of the lecture videos were wholly unhelpful as well. The videos are not substantial enough to teach the content to a level needed to complete the homeworks in my opinion. To complete them, I would go back to reference the lecture videos, only to realize he spent maybe a sentence or two on implementation details we need for the homework, and the rest of the video introing why this technique is important in history, or why it fell out of favor. All in all, the class felt lazy, sloppy, and an absolute nuisance to complete assignments. I strongly recommend against taking CMSC470 with this professor.

review_text: In my opinion, Herman is a vastly underrated professor. He has three midterms and a final, and each is worth about 15-18% of your grade. In terms of lectures, he doesnt allow electronics, which didnt really affect me as I dont use electronics in any of my classes, but he tends to be a pretty good lecturer. He covers the material at a good pace, and is very open to questions about the content. Hes also pretty funny and seems to care about his students imo. He and his TAs have plenty of office hours, and when he didnt have time to cover certain material in class, he went out of his way to make videos about it rather than direct us to the textbook to learn it ourselves, he also gave everyone three pieces of candy for halloween. He does incentivise people to come to lecture and discussion by having "surprise" graded worksheets that are cumulatively worth about 10% of the grade, so if you go to lecture and discussion, you basically get a free 10% of your grade as the worksheets are graded on completion. He also has participation points that are worth 3% of your grade where you basically have to participate a few times over the sem, so another easy 3%. As for projects, none of them were super hard, I think the longest one took me like 3 hours, he released the grades for the first two fairly quickly but waited till the end of the sem for the rest of them. He gives long instructions for the projects which have a lot of helpful details and as long as you follow that and style your code correctly you should be fine, he also gave extra credit for some of them if you finish them before the deadline. Basically, Herman is a good lecturer who cares about his students and gives ample resources and grade boosters so you can get a good grade in the class, just make sure to attend lectures and discussions and you should do fine.

review_text: pedram, the goat that you are... to start off, I want to clarify a couple of things: 1. this was the summer version, so 15 weeks of content condensed to 10 weeks 2. all lectures were recorded bc of this, but there were virtual labs and q&a sessions 3. I never considered myself to be such a visual learner until I took this class. I appreciate that he takes the time to draw both the stack and the heap when explaining concepts such as recursion and the initialization of data structures. I found myself also drawing things out when I wanted to figure out the logic for my projects. he is really great at breaking things down and his slidesets are always very thorough and to the point. I also really liked that he included applications to the real world of what we are learning because it just makes what you're learning a lot cooler yk. projects: the projects that he assigned were somewhat challenging but not to the point where they were impossible. i'd recommend that you just sit with a problem for a while because the answer will come to you eventually if you give yourself enough time. I'm not gonna lie, I lowkey enjoyed them. the projects are pretty much free 100s as long as you submit on time and pass all tests. the content from the projects will basically be most related to what he will test you on the exams, so it's important that you don't chatgpt your way through them. quizzes: idk if this is the case for fall & spring semesters, but our quizzes were not weighted very much and were open note save for the debug quiz (lowkey kinda a joke but appreciated). make sure you do well on them because they're a way to get some easy points. exams: something that pedram does which is such a lifesaver is that he gives an outline of the exam two days prior to it. it contains the methods you will need to know for the exams, what the exam will and will not cover, and how many questions/what type of questions will be present. HYPERFOCUS ON THIS. you don't want to end up spending all your time studying something that won't even be covered. the previous year exams that he gives are good practice, but don't rely entirely on them. simply do the problems related to what the exams will test you on. the exams themselves were pretty fair. since this was a summer class, we had 1 hour and 20 min long exams for the first two exams and then 2 hours for the final. however, our exams were longer since we had more time. for the first time in a cs class ever, I was able to finish an exam in the allotted time for all 3 exams which was a win. I think maybe pedram has changed, but the exams seemed reasonable to complete in the time that he provided. I gotta say that I am not the fastest in terms of algorithmic thinking, but I still felt that I had enough time to complete the coding questions on time. exam structure was generally multiple choice & short answer that tested you on theory, sorting algs (if applicable), and other coding-adjacent concepts like logs and whatnot. the coding questions never require more than 10-15 lines of code to properly fulfill all the requirements for the method. some examples of code-writing questions are completing methods for a class or using data structures to perform certain tasks. all were pretty doable and I'm glad that he tests us on thinking algorithmically bc that's a skill you need as a computer scientist. tips & tricks: - start projects early, but you alr knew that (genuinely it's the best way to actually master concepts from lecture) - also figure out the logic for your projects before your fingers touch the keyboard (will save you lots of strife) - listen to lectures on 2x speed - go over content from exam guidelines religiously - if you lowkey didn't understand anything fom 131 make sure you fully understand the content (I used Alex Lee/Bro Code which I found pretty helpful) - this might be a me thing but don't overtake notes, simply go back to the slides or rewatch lectures as necessary (I found that taking excessive notes were kind of a waste of time) - GO TO DISCUSSION or at least catch up on them immediately if you can't make it since they are essentially mini lectures that cover high-yield content that WILL be tested on exams (ex: sorting algs were taught during discussion which showed up in pretty much every exam) shout out to the TAs! angie, ryan, and brian have saved my life on more than one occassion! this was a pretty memorable class and it's safe to say I feel more confident to take on cs now 😎

review_text: I'll preface my review by stating that I had Dr. Sujeong Kim, but she co-taught this course with Dr. Max Ehrlich, so much of this feedback applies to them both. Starting with the curriculum, I feel that this course was very poorly designed. The professors put in the bare minimum effort, more or less entirely ripping off Berkeley's CS188 course (https://inst.eecs.berkeley.edu/~cs188/fa23/), including all of the topics and slides. In fact, the slides they provided us with were identical to the Berkeley ones, just with the Berkeley branding replaced by UMD branding. They didn't even bother recording lectures, telling us to use the Berkeley recordings instead. Also, the Berkeley course had regular discussions, homeworks, and projects—which would have helped us learn to apply the material we were learning, something the professors didn’t really seem to care about. Moving on to the quality of the lectures, Dr. Kim seems very knowledgeable, but she simply cannot teach effectively and seems best suited for research. Her lectures pretty much consisted of reading off the Berkeley slides and giving inadequate answers when anyone would ask a question. It seems that there was very minimal preparation done before the lectures. The only reason anyone even bothered attending lectures was the clicker quizzes, which effectively made attendance mandatory. I personally learned more putting in headphones and reading the Berkeley notes instead of listening to her. The assignments didn't make the course any better either… There was one midterm exam, which was a disaster. The professors made us take the exam on Gradescope on our laptops in class, because their goal was not to measure students' comprehension of the material but instead to minimize the time and effort needed to grade the exam while maintaining the façade of a well-run class. They provided hardly any review materials themselves and only posted full solutions after complaints on Piazza. And even the solutions provided turned out to have errors. Besides that, they pointed us to Berkeley's past exams, which ended up being nothing like our exam. The exam was such a time crunch that hardly anyone could even finish, and they had to curve the exam to be out of 78 points even though there were well over 100 points originally. The first 2 homework assignments were quite boring, but Homework 3 (a PyTorch lab which involved building an image classifier from scratch) turned out to be quite interesting. However, the professors did not teach us anything to equip us with the knowledge necessary to do the homework. They did not go over how to use PyTorch, how to design a neural network, how convolutional neural networks work, how to improve models, or anything else that would be remotely useful. While this was one of the only thought-provoking assignments, the professors did not prepare us for it at all. Finally, we had a group project due at the end of the semester that was pretty interesting, but the professors did not communicate the requirements clearly at all. They waited until a week before the end of the semester to tell us the details of the final poster presentation and announce that we had to complete a 3-5 page report in addition to the deliverables that we proposed in our project proposals. And that's also when they finally communicated the grading criteria, which was laughable. Somehow, the poster presentation was worth 70%, while the rest of the deliverables combined (including the 3-5 page report and all of the code) were worth just 30%. Overall, it seems like not much thought was put in this course. Why am I paying for a cheap rip-off of a Berkeley course that is freely available to all?

The structure questions on the midterms are similar to the ones on the final. The grading does take a little while but it's not a big deal. As for him answering questions, I didn't have an issue with the ways he answered them, especially with the number of bad questions that were asked (questions like someone asking why put an "x" next to pi when integrating pi in dx terms). To the students who are going to take this course or anything like it: don't blindly ask questions. Actually try to understand it first. I recommend taking Jaime to the people that like a little more independence or already have taken BC calc. If you want a more traditional approach where the prof does all the work, look elsewhere.

review_text: He is not Laxman, he is the LaxGOAT. The class is inherently quite difficult, and the coursework shows it. Expect the homeworks to take you 15-20 hours on the lower end (there was a poll on the piazza that showed 44% of people took >20 hours) and the midterm to thoroughly test your knowledge. Definitely go to lecture too, the recordings are very helpful but the notes can be hard to follow. Laxman was incredibly understanding throughout the entire semester and continually offered deadline extensions and waived late penalties to help with the workload. Furthermore, the actual course content is very interesting. Not only are the algorithms taught (somewhat) applicable to interviews and the job setting, but I left the semester with a much better foundation of how to think about solving algorithmic problems. I would 100% take any class this professor teaches.
evidence_snippet: homeworks to take you 15-20 hours
label_rationale: Homework is extremely time-consuming, while the professor is understanding and fair.

review_text: I am writing this review for Math140 and Math141: Pretty good professor. Explains concepts well and gives lots of practice to prepare for exams. Takes questions from webassigns, discussion, and lecture and puts mostly similar ones on the exams. There’s 5 exams total including the final which means each exam (excluding the final) doesn’t have an overwhelming amount of content. He gives you a few drops for lowest quizzes, discussion worksheets and webassigns which is nice. The quizzes were frequent and a bit annoying but did help me keep up with the material. (There were no quizzes in calc 1 but were in calc 2). Discussion worksheets weren’t too bad because we get to work in groups but honestly felt useless as they weren’t really good practice in my opinion. He could do a lot to help students like recording lectures (he recorded them for calc 1 but not calc 2) or making the discussion worksheets doable from home as some students live off campus and showing up for 1 worksheet (that doesn’t even help understand the concepts if im being honest) is frustrating. He was much more friendly and energetic in calc 2 although it could just be the section I took (morning calc 1 vs afternoon calc 2) Speaks clearly and answers questions. TLDR: Not a bad class or prof. Could be improved a little bit but good enough where if you put effort you should pass. You may be better taking it with someone else if you’re not the best with math.

review_text: My review won't be as critical as the other one for this semester, but I share a lot of the sentiments about Pete and the class. Pete himself admitted that his info about this topic in general is out of date one class, and his generally subpar lecturing style (very monotone) leads to a lot of confusion and difficulty understanding content. We follow an online (free) textbook which goes into more detail, but a lot of the content on the exams is either difficult to find in the textbook or just something he put on a couple slides. The exams themselves aren't difficult given you scour the slides and your notes. All the problems on the exam are either short form questions about certain topics or definitions, or questions you've seen before on homeworks. The projects are on the more difficult side compared to other 4XX classes, and set up similar to 417 where they're tangentially related to what we're currently learning about in class, but most of the work is figuring out how to implement the features within the existing GeekOS system. I personally really enjoyed these projects, they were interesting and fun to work with. The difference though between this class and 417 though, is that the project specs are rather useless. They don't really help much with understanding what you're doing at all to be honest, and its hard to get a grasp of the scope of each project purely from the spec sheets. It's not impossible, but there's a noticeable difference that leads to a worse experience. However, the issues with projects is all offset by the TA Leo. For every project, he provided a video and slides that allowed us to work our way through each project step by step. He gave us good tips and ideas during OH, and basically led the project part of the course.
